content: Subjects who maintained a consistently normal BMI throughout their lives exhibited lower risks of developing hypertension in adulthood. In contrast, individuals who were obese as adults, regardless of their childhood adiposity status (Groups III and IV), demonstrated a significantly increased risk of hypertension in adulthood. Two studies specifically examined the influence of childhood BMI on adult hypertension. The East Boston Blood Pressure Study revealed that an increase in childhood BMI percentile was associated with a heightened risk of hypertension in adulthood. Similarly, data from the 1958 British Cohort Study indicated a significant relationship between BMI at age 16 and changes in BMI between ages 7 and 16 with the development of hypertension in adulthood. Regarding systolic blood pressure (SBP), 14 studies (from 12 cohorts) identified associations between childhood and adolescent anthropometric measures and SBP in later life. These measures included height, weight, BMI, ponderal index, waist circumference, and skinfold thickness. Ten cohorts demonstrated a relationship between BMI and SBP, seven cohorts linked weight to hypertension, and seven cohorts associated height with SBP. The Longitudinal Study of Juvenile Hypertension explored the relationship between skinfold thickness and SBP, while one cohort addressed the age of adiposity rebound and its connection to SBP. The Vulnerable Window Cohort 1 study found a positive association between BMI during early childhood (6 months to 2 years) and SBP in later childhood (2–11 years). Another study from the 1958 British Birth Cohort identified a significant association between BMI at age 16 and adult SBP levels, as well as changes in BMI between ages 7 and 16. Notably, individuals in the thinnest 10% of the population at ages 11 and 16 exhibited higher adult SBP levels. The Northern Finland Birth Cohort 42 study observed a significant association between BMI in infancy and adult SBP levels in individuals within the 90th to 95th percentiles. Conversely, the New Delhi Birth Cohort study found a significant relationship between changes in conditional BMI during infancy and adult SBP. Five additional studies from various cohorts confirmed a significant association between childhood BMI and increased adult SBP. However, the Newcastle Thousand Families Cohort Study reported an inverse relationship between childhood BMI and adult SBP. The Northern Finland Birth Cohort 111 study measured BMI at adiposity rebound and found no association with adult SBP. Two studies from the Vulnerable Windows Cohort 1 and the Avon Longitudinal Study of Parents and Children (ALSPAC) demonstrated a positive association between infant weight and childhood SBP (ages 10 and 11). The Peruvian Birth Cohort study found no association between infant weight and adolescent SBP but identified an inverse relationship after adjusting for adolescent weight. Additionally, two studies from different cohorts reported a positive association between childhood weight and adult SBP. The New Delhi Birth Cohort study also observed a positive association between conditional weight in infancy and adult weight. Two studies from ALSPAC and the Vulnerable Windows Cohort Study 1 identified a positive association between infant height and higher SBP in mid-childhood (ages 10 and 11). The 1946 British Birth Cohort study observed a positive association between height at age 2 and adult SBP. A longitudinal study of juvenile hypertension found a weak positive association between childhood height and adult SBP in males, but a weak negative association in females. The Minneapolis Children’s Blood Pressure Study demonstrated a positive association between childhood height and adult SBP. The Northern Finland Birth Cohort 1966 study found that peak height velocity exceeding 8 cm/year during infancy was associated with an increased risk of adult SBP. However, the Peruvian Birth Cohort study found no association between infant height and adult SBP. Two studies, the Bogalusa Heart Study and the Longitudinal Study of Juvenile Hypertension, identified a positive association between adolescent skinfold thickness and increased adult SBP. However, the NHLBI study found no association between the sum of skinfold thickness at age 9 and adolescent SBP. Two studies from NHLBI and ALSPAC found a significant association between waist circumference at age 9 and adolescent SBP. A rapid increase in waist circumference was associated with higher odds of developing elevated SBP later in adolescence. Regarding diastolic blood pressure (DBP), 14 articles (from 10 cohorts) analyzed the relationship between childhood and adolescent anthropometric measures and adult DBP levels. These measures included height, weight, BMI, waist circumference, skinfold thickness, and age at adiposity rebound. Eight of the 10 cohorts were based in developed countries, while the remaining two were from lowand middle-income countries (Peru and China). The Bogalusa Heart Study found a positive association between childhood BMI and adult DBP levels. Three articles identified a positive relationship between adolescent BMI and adult DBP levels. The Northern Finland Birth Cohort 1966 study categorized childhood BMI by percentiles and found that individuals in the highest percentile (>95th) had a higher risk of elevated adult DBP levels. The 1958 British Birth Cohort study stratified adult BMI by childhood and adolescent BMI and found that adults in the leanest 10% during childhood and adolescence had the highest DBP levels in adulthood. Two articles reported that greater increases in BMI during childhood (ages 2–10) and adolescence (ages 11–16) were positively associated with adult DBP levels. The ALSPAC study did not find any association between BMI increases from late childhood to adolescence and adult DBP levels. Similarly, the Hong Kong Birth Cohort of 1967 found no association between BMI changes during and after infancy (6–18 months) and adult DBP levels. Two studies demonstrated that the positive association between childhood BMI and adult DBP levels was reversed after adjusting for adult BMI levels. Another two studies from the Bogalusa Heart Study found that adult DBP levels correlated with the tracking of childhood obesity into adulthood. The ALSPAC study established a strong positive relationship between post-infancy weight and weight-for-height and childhood (age 10) DBP levels. The Longitudinal Study of Juvenile Hypertension found a weak positive association between adolescent weight and adult DBP levels. The Peruvian Birth Cohort study did not find any association between weight-for-length in infancy and early childhood and adolescent DBP levels. The Northern Finland Birth Cohort of 1966 demonstrated that greater weight gain in infancy was associated with higher adult DBP levels, but this relationship was reversed after adjusting for adult BMI. The same cohort found that a greater increase in height during infancy was associated with higher adult DBP levels, even after adjusting for adult BMI. The ALSPAC study did not find any association between post-infancy height and adolescent DBP levels, and similar results were observed in the Peruvian Birth Cohort. The Longitudinal Study of Juvenile Hypertension found a weak positive relationship between adolescent height and adult DBP levels in males and a weak negative relationship in females. The Bogalusa Heart Study found a positive correlation between childhood triceps skinfold thickness and adult DBP levels. The National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute Growth and Health Study (NGHS) demonstrated a positive relationship between the sum of skinfold thickness at age 9 and the increase in DBP levels from ages 12 to 14. The Longitudinal Study of Juvenile Hypertension established a weak positive association between adolescent triceps skinfold thickness and adult DBP. They also found a strong positive correlation between subscapular skinfold thickness and adult DBP levels in females only. The ALSPAC study established a positive relationship between a rapid increase in waist circumference from late childhood (ages 9–12) to adolescence (ages 15–16) and DBP levels in adolescence. The NGHS demonstrated that waist circumference at age 9 was associated with an increase in DBP levels from ages 12 to 14. The Northern Finland Birth Cohort of 1966 study established that an earlier age at adiposity rebound was associated with higher DBP levels in adulthood, but no relationship was found between BMI at adiposity rebound and adult DBP levels.
